label: sec:nn-isospin-interface-intro
html:
Nature offers four two-nucleon channels and binds exactly one of them. Three --- pp, nn, and the symmetric pn state --- carry total isospin T = 1 and are unbound; the antisymmetric pn state, the deuteron, carries T = 0 and binds at 2.224566\ \mathrm{MeV}. Any account of nuclear binding in this framework has to reproduce that pattern before it reproduces a number.

Two mechanisms are in play, and this section keeps them apart because they are distinct objects.

The isospin mechanism selects. It assigns each channel the Wedderburn weight of its isospin block, \mu_+ for the triplet and \mu_- for the singlet, and the ordering \mu_- < \mu_+ holds identically in q under convention D. With binding B = -\alpha\log\mu, decreasing in \mu, the singlet is always the more strongly bound channel. No multiplicity is counted and no parameter is tuned.

The interface mechanism produces the number. A single inter-nucleon bond contributes a Markov scalar \mu = z + d with d ranging over the admissible interval [-h, 0], and the binding follows from the same logarithm. This is the mechanism the mass pipeline actually evaluates.

The section proceeds in that order: the ordering that selects the channel, the refutation of the alternative it replaces, the selection map on colour systems, the branching identity that ties the isospin weights to the algebra, and then the measurement of where the interface band sits relative to the two weights. The answer to the last question is negative and sharp --- the band lies strictly between \mu_- and \mu_+, so no admissible interface element realises either --- which is why the two mechanisms must be described as computing on disjoint sets rather than as two views of one computation.
